# Technographic APIs for preparing consultancy sales conversations

I would evaluate TheirStack and PredictLeads first. Both expose evidence and recency that can make an inferred stack claim inspectable. HG Insights is a further enterprise option; Coresignal and GitHub provide building blocks if you need tighter control over the evidence. This ranking reflects the documented fit to the request, not a measured accuracy comparison.

The central qualification is that public signals rarely establish a complete current internal stack. A job advertisement can describe current use, desired experience, a migration or work for a client. Prepare a conversation with a dated observation and an open question, rather than treating an inferred tool as a confirmed company-wide deployment.

## Ranked candidates

### 1. TheirStack Company Technographics API

[Company Technographics endpoint](https://theirstack.com/en/docs/api-reference/companies/technographics_v1)

TheirStack documents a company lookup returning technologies, confidence levels, job-mention counts and first/last mention dates. That is a useful starting point for finding internal engineering tools and prioritizing recent, repeated evidence. Its [sourcing explanation](https://theirstack.com/en/docs/data/technographic/how-we-source-tech-stack-data) says the inference comes from job postings and explains the confidence signals.

For this consultancy, I would check a representative list of target CI/CD and security products against known accounts. Do not interpret an absent result as proof that the company lacks a tool: the sourcing page explicitly acknowledges that tools can go unmentioned and companies may not be hiring.

### 2. PredictLeads Technology Detections and Extended Technology Detections

[Technology detection documentation](https://docs.predictleads.com/v3/guide/technology_detections_dataset/api_endpoints)

PredictLeads offers company/domain technology lookups and an extended dataset explaining detection clues from jobs, web subpages, DNS and connections. The schema includes first/last observation dates and source-related fields. This is attractive when a salesperson needs to inspect why a tool appears in a prospect's profile.

Its [official n8n integration](https://github.com/PredictLeads/n8n-nodes-predict-leads) can retrieve company technologies and jobs, which could help assemble a repeatable pre-call workflow. It requires provider credentials. Validate the underlying clues and specific product coverage; a detection remains evidence to interpret.

### 3. HG Insights Technographics API

[Technographic install-record guide](https://data-docs.hginsights.com/v2/guides/understanding-hg-data)

HG documents product-level installation records with vendor and category information, first/last verification dates, country, intensity and location counts. These fields could help investigate enterprise accounts and separate a stale observation from a recently verified product record.

Ask for representative CI/CD and security matches before committing to the service; the public documentation does not establish accuracy for your account list. The [API overview](https://help.hginsights.com/docs/hg-api) was published in April 2026 but updated in October and now discusses a September API retirement. I therefore preserve this reviewed version as later evidence, not a verified July 2026 implementation choice.

### 4. Coresignal Jobs API

[Jobs API](https://coresignal.com/solutions/jobs-data-api/)

This is an alternative building block if you want to own the interpretation. Coresignal documents structured job records, company and posting-date filters, and multi-source deduplication. It explicitly identifies technology signals as a use case.

A narrow extraction pipeline could recognize your consultancy's CI/CD and security product vocabulary, retain the matching context, and distinguish explicit usage from preferred experience or planned migration. That proposed pipeline is my application of the source, not a verified built-in Coresignal capability. It needs engineering and review, but lets you control which observations become sales assertions.

### 5. GitHub Actions REST API for public workflows and runs

[Workflow API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/actions/workflows) · [Workflow-run API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/actions/workflow-runs)

GitHub documents public read access to workflow metadata and execution records. For a company with an independently verified public organization, this can provide concrete corroboration of CI/CD practice in particular repositories. Recent runs help distinguish active workflows from abandoned configuration.

This is a supplement with narrow coverage. A public library's workflow does not establish the company's private production pipeline, and workflow metadata alone cannot enumerate its security products. Company attribution and repository relevance need checking before using the observation in a conversation.

## How I would evaluate and use the results

Choose a small sample of companies whose stack you can independently check. Compare each provider on the tools that matter to your consultancy, freshness, inspectable supporting evidence and the rate of ambiguous matches. Include accounts with little public hiring activity so the sample does not hide coverage gaps.

For each proposed conversation point, retain the company identifier, technology, observation date, source type, supporting link and interpretation. Separate an explicit statement of current use from a hiring requirement or an inference. An LLM can summarize retrieved evidence, but require it to leave unsupported technologies unknown and preserve the source for each material claim.

I did not access any paid API, register an account or test accuracy against real company records. These are verified documentation-level candidates and proposed applications, not proof of deployment or usefulness. The public code-search endpoint was inaccessible; the official PredictLeads integration was found and opened through a clearly labelled code-through-web fallback.

The question's cutoff is July 12, 2026. Other than the later HG overview, the opened documentation is live and undated, so its availability and exact behavior at that cutoff remain unknown. The search was conducted on November 21, 2026.

I would evaluate **NLog first and Apache log4net second**. Both offer the SQL-plus-local-file arrangement you described and accept an exception object directly. They are logging libraries you integrate into the existing C#/WPF application.

## 1. NLog

[NLog](https://nlog-project.org/) is the first alternative I would try. Its documented targets include files and databases, and the same event can be sent to multiple destinations. That matches the shape of your requirement: keep a local file target enabled alongside the database target.

For SQL output, [DatabaseTarget](https://nlog-project.org/documentation/v6.0.0/html/T_NLog_Targets_DatabaseTarget.htm) uses an ADO.NET provider and configurable SQL commands and parameters. The documentation inspected here places it in the NLog.Database assembly. You still need a compatible database provider, connection settings, a table, and the mapping from event fields to SQL parameters.

For the exception itself, the [Error(Exception, String) API](https://nlog-project.org/documentation/v6.0.0/html/M_NLog_Logger_Error_3.htm) lets application code pass the exception as an object:

```csharp
logger.Error(ex, "Saving the record failed");
```

You therefore do not have to break an exception into separate properties at every call site. Select an output layout that includes the exception information you want retained. Database-column mapping is still configuration work; accepting an exception object does not automatically design your SQL table.

NLog's overview lists .NET Framework and modern .NET support. Your exact target framework is unspecified, so check the chosen NLog and database-provider package versions against the WPF project's target framework.

## 2. Apache log4net

[Apache log4net's AdoNetAppender](https://logging.apache.org/log4net/manual/configuration/appenders/adonetappender.html) documents database logging, including a SQL Server configuration with parameterized inserts and an ExceptionLayout for the exception column. Pair that with [RollingFileAppender](https://logging.apache.org/log4net/manual/configuration/appenders/rollingfileappender.html) for local files with size- or date-based rotation. Its [FAQ](https://logging.apache.org/log4net/log4net-2.0.8/release/faq.html) confirms that a logger can have multiple output appenders.

The [ILog.Error(Object, Exception) API](https://logging.apache.org/log4net/log4net-2.0.8/release/sdk/html/M_log4net_ILog_Error_1.htm) takes the exception directly and includes its stack trace:

```csharp
log.Error("Saving the record failed", ex);
```

This is a concrete second option if its logger/appender configuration model suits your application. The current [framework support table](https://logging.apache.org/log4net/manual/supported-frameworks.html) lists the relevant database and file appenders for .NET Framework 4.6.2 and .NET Standard 2.0. That is evidence for those documented targets, not a blanket promise for every historical .NET version.

## Configuration point that matters for your SQL-error case

Configure the local file as an independently enabled destination, alongside SQL logging. Do not make producing the only local diagnostic depend on a successful database insert. This is an implementation recommendation based on the documented multiple-destination facilities, not a claim that I have tested your application.

During evaluation, deliberately cause the application's database operation to fail and confirm that the exception still reaches the local log. Also test an unavailable logging database. Check the chosen path's write permission, exception layout, buffering, and shutdown behavior. The log4net FAQ explicitly describes delivery as best effort; neither the documents inspected nor this review establish lossless delivery during crashes or storage failure.

I would keep your existing Serilog experience as the comparison baseline and make the decision from a small NLog-versus-log4net trial using those failure cases. I have not established Python support for either recommendation, and I have treated it as the optional benefit you described.

**Evidence limits:** This is a documentation-based shortlist, not an executed integration. The question is dated January 10, 2023; several accessible sources are undated live manuals, and the NLog API pages describe version 6.0, which is later than that decision date. These sources establish the documented capabilities of the versions shown; they do not reconstruct every package/version combination available on the original question date.

# Authentik federation versus separate passwords and 2FA

Moving login to Authentik does not inherently give every application the same reusable credential. OpenID Connect distinguishes the identity provider, each relying application, and the ID token issued for that application; OAuth access tokens have a separate resource-access purpose. A token should only be accepted by its intended recipient. This makes the phrase “one stolen token” too broad to determine the impact. The relevant token might be an application session cookie, an application-specific ID/access token, a refresh token, or Authentik's own browser session. [OpenID Connect Core](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0-errata1.html) and [Authentik's provider documentation](https://docs.goauthentik.io/add-secure-apps/providers/oauth2/) establish those protocol roles.

The central risk is a shared authentication authority. My inference is that an attacker holding a usable Authentik session may obtain access to additional applications wherever their policies accept that session without fresh verification. Compromise of the identity provider's administrative or signing authority is a broader failure again. By comparison, genuinely independent service passwords and second factors can contain a single service-account compromise, assuming the other credentials and recovery paths remain independent. Neither architecture supplies a universal security ranking without knowing the applications, their session handling, and the attack being considered.

## Ranked reusable designs and mechanisms

### 1. OpenID Connect Core 1.0: application-specific identity tokens and reauthentication

URL: https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0-errata1.html

Use this standard to check whether each application has its own client registration, validates the intended audience, and requests fresh authentication for sensitive access. The ID token's audience includes the relying party's client ID, while max_age and auth_time support an explicit freshness requirement. This directly addresses whether a token stolen from service A should work at service B.

Caveat: an ID token is not an access token or a universal session cookie; merely using a JWT does not establish correct recipient validation. Freshness also depends on what authentication the provider actually requires.

Date evidence: the opened errata-1 specification is dated 8 November 2014, before the 28 March 2025 cutoff.

### 2. Authentik Authenticator Validation stage: retain mandatory MFA centrally

URL: https://docs.goauthentik.io/add-secure-apps/flows-stages/stages/authenticator_validate

This component helps preserve the existing second-factor requirement when moving authentication into Authentik. Its configurable device classes, enrollment behavior, and last-validation threshold let the authentication flow require an accepted factor and control when a recent verification may be reused. For accounts with no eligible authenticator, configure enrollment or denial instead of allowing the flow to skip MFA.

Caveat: placing MFA in a login flow does not prove that every application access reruns it. Verify the relevant provider flow and session behavior; an already-authorized application session can have its own lifetime. Authentik's [hardening guidance](https://docs.goauthentik.io/security/security-hardening) also calls out recovery flows as part of the account's security boundary.

Date evidence: live documentation; the exact configuration described here was not established from a dated pre-cutoff version.

### 3. RFC 9700: restricted tokens and a hardened OAuth authorization flow

URL: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9700

Use this security baseline to limit token consequences: restrict access-token audiences and privileges, use authorization code flow with PKCE where applicable, and protect refresh tokens with client binding, rotation, or sender constraint. Its audience rule specifically requires a resource server to reject a token intended for a different resource server.

Caveat: PKCE protects the code exchange; it is not a cure for theft of an already-issued bearer token or an authenticated browser session. Every application must enforce the relevant checks. The document is a standard, not evidence that a particular deployment already implements it.

Date evidence: RFC 9700 was published in January 2025, before the cutoff.

### 4. Authentik User Login stage: bound the shared identity-provider session

URL: https://docs.goauthentik.io/add-secure-apps/flows-stages/stages/user_login/

This component exposes the lifetime and reuse controls for the Authentik session itself, including session duration, remember-me extension, termination of other sessions, and optional network or location binding. These are directly relevant to the credential whose compromise could enable fresh logins to several applications.

Caveat: the documentation explicitly separates termination of Authentik sessions from OAuth refresh tokens. Browser-session cookies may survive browser behavior that users interpret as closing the browser, and location binding is not cryptographic replay prevention. Set and test the identity-provider session, application session, and token lifetimes separately.

Date evidence: live documentation, with no dated version opened to establish these exact details before the cutoff.

### 5. WebAuthn Level 2: origin-scoped public-key authentication

URL: https://www.w3.org/TR/2021/REC-webauthn-2-20210408/

WebAuthn provides public-key credentials scoped to the relying party, making it a useful stronger authentication mechanism at the central identity provider or independently at especially sensitive applications. Its origin and credential scoping address credential phishing rather than relying only on a reusable password or manually entered one-time code. Authentik's current validation-stage documentation supports WebAuthn and a user-verification requirement.

Caveat: protecting the authentication ceremony does not invalidate an already-stolen authenticated session. Enrollment, spare authenticators, and recovery need to preserve the same security objective. Independent registration at an application requires that application's support.

Date evidence: the opened W3C Recommendation is dated 8 April 2021, before the cutoff; the separate Authentik integration evidence is live documentation.

### 6. OpenID Connect Back-Channel Logout 1.0: propagate session termination

URL: https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-backchannel-1_0.html

This protocol gives the identity provider a direct server-to-server mechanism for asking relying applications to terminate sessions, which can make central incident response more useful after session theft or account compromise. It addresses the gap between ending the identity-provider session and ending each application's own session.

Caveat: the relying application must implement session termination and expose a logout endpoint reachable by the provider. It does not automatically revoke every independent bearer token. Confirm support and behavior for each installed application and provider version.

Date evidence: the opened specification incorporates errata set 1 and is dated 15 December 2023, before the cutoff.

### 7. RFC 9449 DPoP: make a stolen token insufficient by itself

URL: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9449

DPoP is an alternative to ordinary bearer-token replay semantics: the client proves possession of a private key and the recipient verifies the token's binding to that key. It can reduce the value of a leaked access or refresh token when the attacker has not also obtained the corresponding key or control of the client.

Caveat: this requires compatible clients, authorization servers, and resource servers. I did not establish that the user's Authentik deployment or applications support it, and it does not protect an unrelated Authentik browser cookie.

Date evidence: RFC 9449 was published in September 2023, before the cutoff.

## How I would use this shortlist

For a practical comparison, trace four independent paths: a compromised service account, a stolen application's token/session, a stolen Authentik session, and compromise of Authentik's administrative authority. For each, identify which other applications become accessible, whether another factor is required, and how access is revoked. This is a design review framework rather than a claim about a tested installation.

The most immediately transferable controls are separate application registrations, mandatory MFA with suitable recovery, recipient-restricted tokens, explicit session lifetimes, and verified logout behavior. Keeping additional local authentication for a particularly sensitive application is a reasonable isolation option if that application's access path actually enforces it. Federation can improve consistency and management while concentrating trust; retaining independent credentials trades that concentration for more separate authentication and recovery systems to maintain.

All seven candidate sources were opened. An unauthenticated grep.app code-search attempt failed; a public GitHub source page was subsequently found through web search and opened, so that is code-through-web evidence, not native code-search success. Current Authentik documentation and main-branch code are not treated as proof of March 2025 behavior. No deployment, exploit test, or empirical security comparison was performed.

candidate_links.name: OpenID Connect Core 1.0: application-specific identity tokens and reauthentication
RFC 9700 OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice
Authentik User Login stage session controls

I would investigate **KeeWeb with your own Docker-hosted WebDAV storage first**, followed by **Psono** and **self-hosted Bitwarden**. I cannot certify any of these as satisfying your master-password-hash rule literally from the documentation I verified. That condition needs a more precise storage check than the usual claim that a product is self-hosted or encrypts passwords.

I interpret “furryfox” as Firefox, and “no intermediary” as keeping the password-service and authentication path under your control while allowing the cloud infrastructure you explicitly mentioned.

### 1. KeeWeb plus your own WebDAV container

This is the most promising architecture for avoiding an intermediary password service. KeeWeb works with encrypted KDBX files and documents Windows and Linux desktop clients. Its official release page includes a Linux .deb package, and KeeWeb Connect lists Chrome and Firefox extensions. The desktop release evidence includes artifacts dated July 2021, before your June 2023 question. See the [official repository](https://github.com/keeweb/keeweb), [desktop releases](https://github.com/keeweb/keeweb/releases) and [extension repository](https://github.com/keeweb/keeweb-connect).

The concrete arrangement would be: run a WebDAV server in a Docker container on your cloud machine, keep the KDBX file in that server's persistent storage, and configure the desktop clients to open that file from your own server. KeeWeb's [WebDAV guide](https://github.com/keeweb/keeweb/wiki/WebDAV-Setup) documents such containerized storage. Serving the KeeWeb web application from a container alone does not supply this vault-storage component.

The [FAQ](https://github.com/keeweb/keeweb/wiki/FAQ) describes local operation and network transfer only when requested. That supports the architecture, but it does not prove that every persistent password-derived verifier in the desktop application, extension, and cache is confined to the KDBX file. Use a separate WebDAV login credential and verify the selected clients' stored state. Chrome compatibility also needs a version-specific check: the official README advertises Chrome, but a later issue snippet reports trouble with Chrome 131. That report is dated December 2024 and cannot establish a failure at your 2023 decision date.

**Verdict: promising, but verification required.** It is a composed application-and-storage solution. Confirmation that no prohibited verifier is persisted elsewhere, together with compatible browser versions, could make it a documented fit; a confirmed out-of-vault hash would rule it out under your literal requirement.

### 2. Psono, with the server and database under your control

### 3. Bitwarden, self-hosted

Yes. For the English/plain-text case you described, I would start with **GNU `tr`**, or use **Python's standard library** if you want different random output each time. Both approaches can preserve the original word lengths exactly, which is stronger than the approximate match you asked for.

## 1. GNU tr: the simplest ready command

Use an ASCII ROT13 substitution:

```sh
LC_ALL=C tr 'A-Za-z' 'N-ZA-Mn-za-m' < input.txt > gibberish.txt
```

This replaces each uppercase or lowercase English letter with another letter. Spaces, punctuation, and line breaks are outside the translation set, so they stay in their original positions. Every word keeps exactly the same number of letters. For example, `Hello, world!` becomes `Uryyb, jbeyq!`.

The opened [GNU tr manpage packaged by Debian](https://manpages.debian.org/bullseye/coreutils/tr.1.en.html) documents character-set translation and identifies the software as GPLv3+. The command above applies those documented operations; I have not executed it as part of this review.

ROT13 is deterministic and reversible. It produces letter-substitution gibberish, with no promise that every individual result is a nonword or that it sounds pronounceable. Your question does not require either randomness or pronounceability, so this is a practical fit for the stated requirements. Equal character counts also do not imply identical widths in a proportional font.

## 2. Python re + random: fresh random letters

For a library-based solution, the standard library is sufficient. [re.sub](https://docs.python.org/3.10/library/re.html#re.sub) can call a function for each matched letter, and [random.choice](https://docs.python.org/3.10/library/random.html#random.choice) can select its replacement.

Save the following as `gibberish.py`:

```python
import random
import re
import sys

lowercase = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"

def replace_letter(match):
    letter = match.group()
    pool = lowercase.upper() if letter.isupper() else lowercase
    return random.choice(pool.replace(letter, ""))

text = sys.stdin.buffer.read().decode("utf-8")
result = re.sub(r"[A-Za-z]", replace_letter, text)
sys.stdout.buffer.write(result.encode("utf-8"))
```

Then run:

```sh
python3 gibberish.py < input.txt > gibberish.txt
```

Each matched letter is replaced by one different letter of the same case. Because the pattern contains only ASCII letters, punctuation, digits, spaces, and line breaks remain where they were. The binary input/output wrapper avoids newline conversion. These preservation properties follow from the supplied implementation and documented APIs; this particular script was not run during the review.

Python's official documentation covers [Linux availability](https://docs.python.org/3.10/using/unix.html) and its [open-source license](https://docs.python.org/3.10/license.html). The output consists of random letter strings, so use this when the requested “look” means the word lengths and separators described in your question, rather than pronounceable invented language.

## An unconfirmed browser option

[Thinkzone's Gibberish Generator](https://thinkzone.wlonk.com/Gibber/GibGen.html) accepts input text and creates gibberish from character-sequence statistics. I would not yet choose it for this task: its documentation does not establish matching each original word's length, and it cautions about paired punctuation and whitespace. Its JavaScript source could not be opened in this review, leaving those properties, the code-license scope, and explicit Linux support unconfirmed. It remains a lead to check, not a verified substitute for the two approaches above.

The date evidence also has limits. The tr page identifies a September 2020 source version, although its HTML rendition was generated later. Python 3.10.7 was [released on September 6, 2022](https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-3107/), before your question, but the API pages retrieved now are live documentation rather than frozen September 2022 copies.
